content: 1. The proportion of first-time testers among partners or social contacts of individuals who inject drugs was higher in the Social Network Approach (SNA) group compared to the non-SNA group. Specifically, there were 13 more first-time testers per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 2 more to 35 more). However, the certainty of this evidence is low due to critical limitations. 2. The study by Kan et al. (quasi-experimental) was downgraded due to reliance on self-reported data, which introduces a risk of bias. Additionally, inconsistency could not be assessed as the findings were based on a single study. 3. Chiou et al. (quasi-experimental) used propensity matching in their final analyses, but the data were self-reported, leading to a downgrade in the certainty of evidence due to potential bias. 4. Pines et al. (quasi-experimental) employed Poisson regression analysis, but the reliance on self-reported data resulted in a downgrade in the certainty of evidence due to bias. 5. Gwadz et al. (non-randomized parallel study design) did not control for confounders and experienced a 25% loss of participants in the second session of the respondent-driven sampling confidential two-session testing (RDS-CTT) group. These limitations led to a downgrade in the certainty of evidence. 6. Hall et al. (quasi-experimental) relied on self-reported data, which introduced bias. Furthermore, there was no information provided about missing data or loss to follow-up, leading to a downgrade in the certainty of evidence. 7. Schumann et al. (quasi-experimental) did not statistically control for confounders. The study eligibility criteria were vaguely defined as at-risk individuals, and inclusion criteria were not clearly specified. Some recruiters exceeded the pre-intervention cap of 20 social network clients. Additionally, there was no information on how missing data were handled, resulting in a downgrade in the certainty of evidence. 8. Skaathun et al. (cohort study) was downgraded due to the use of three different testing methods at different time periods: routine hospital-based testing (2011–2016), risk network strategy (2013–2016), and respondent-driven sampling (2013–2014). This temporal variation introduced a risk of selection bias and potential confounding due to secular trends. 9. Guo et al. (quasi-experimental) relied on self-reported data, which introduced bias and led to a downgrade in the certainty of evidence. 10. Halkitis et al. (quasi-experimental) also relied on self-reported data, resulting in a downgrade in the certainty of evidence. 11. Four out of six studies reported a significantly higher percentage of individuals testing positive for HIV using the Social Network Approach (SNA). However, the certainty of evidence was affected by study design limitations and potential biases. 12. The cost per person tested using SNA versus non-SNA methods varied across studies. For example, Skaathun et al. reported a cost of $1,142, Pines et al. reported $260, and Zulliger et al. reported $584. The certainty of evidence was moderate due to differences in study perspectives and healthcare systems. 13. The cost per person diagnosed with HIV also varied. Skaathun et al. reported $15,683, Pines et al. reported $5,273, and Zulliger et al. reported $16,949. The certainty of evidence was moderate, with differences explained by study perspectives and healthcare systems. 14. The cost per person tested using different types of SNA was assessed. For example, SNA with HIV self-testing (HIVST) was compared to SNA with testing referral cards. The cost per person tested was $120 versus $94, respectively. The certainty of evidence was moderate. 15. The cost per person diagnosed using SNA with financial incentives versus SNA without financial incentives was $1,538 versus $930, respectively. The certainty of evidence was moderate. 16. The cost per person diagnosed using SNA with HIVST versus SNA with testing referral cards was not estimable in one study. The certainty of evidence was moderate. 17. Differences in study designs, perspectives, and healthcare systems contributed to variations in findings. For example, Skaathun et al. and Pines et al. used a healthcare provider’s perspective, while Zulliger et al. adopted a societal perspective. These differences were considered when assessing the certainty of evidence. 18. Some studies, such as Shahmanesh et al., did not verify whether distributed HIVST kits were used, reporting only the cost per kit distributed. This introduced indirectness and lowered the certainty of evidence. 19. Inconsistencies between studies were generally explainable by differences in the type of SNA implemented or the healthcare systems in which the studies were conducted. For example, studies conducted in China and South Africa differed in their comparators and implementation strategies. 20. Imprecision was noted in some studies due to low event rates (<400 events), which led to downgrades in the certainty of evidence.
